Appendix A Appendix Overview

This appendix provides a rigorous theoretical foundation, comprehensive empirical validation, and detailed implementation specifics for Attention Contrastive Decoding (ACD). The content is organized as follows:

  • •

    Theoretical Analysis: Smoothness of Attention-Level Operations (Section B): Establishes the mathematical framework for ACD, providing dimension-independent perturbation bounds and proving why attention-level interventions yield smoother output distributions than logit-level contrastive decoding.

  • •

    Empirical Validation of Distribution Smoothness (Section C): validates the theoretical propositions through total variation (TV) distance and KL divergence analysis, demonstrating ACD’s superior temporal stability and distributional coherence.

  • •

    Robustness to Contrastive Strength (Section D): Presents ablation studies confirming ACD’s stability across varying hyperparameters (α\alpha), supported by the theoretical scaling analysis.

  • •

    Decoding Procedure (Section E): Delineates the algorithmic implementation of ACD (Algorithm 1), detailing the dual-attention cache mechanism and the Adaptive Subtraction Strategy.

  • •

    Layer-wise Propagation and Semantic Alignment (Section F): Analyzes the residual stream dynamics to explain how modality-dependent perturbations propagate through transformer layers while remaining bounded.

  • •

    More Related Work (Section G): Reviews the landscape of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) and positioning this work within the broader context of hallucination mitigation.

  • •

    Benchmarks and Evaluation Metrics (Section H): Details the experimental setup, including protocols for CHAIR, LLaVA-Bench, POPE, and MME benchmarks.

  • •

    Efficiency Comparison (Section I): Benchmarks the computational overhead, demonstrating that ACD reduces latency and memory usage compared to standard VCD.

  • •

    Additional Experimental Results (Sections J & K): Reports comprehensive performance on the full MME suite and analyzes scalability across 7B and 13B parameter models.

  • •

    Ablation on Sampling Strategies (Section L): Examines the interaction between ACD and various decoding methods (Greedy, Top-kk, Top-pp, etc.), confirming strategy-agnostic improvements.

  • •

    Additional Validation Experiments (Section M): Presents ASS threshold sensitivity analysis, a stratified analysis of ACD’s effect on clean versus hallucinating instances, comprehensive Qwen3-VL (2025) results on MME and POPE, and an analysis of VCD degeneration on deeper architectures.

  • •

    Qualitative Analysis and Setup (Sections N & O): Provides visual case studies of hallucination correction and details the GPT-5 evaluation prompts used for open-ended assessment.

Appendix B Theoretical Analysis: Smoothness of Attention-Level Operations

We provide rigorous theoretical justification for why attention-level contrastive operations produce smoother output distributions than logit-level interventions. Our analysis establishes: (1) dimension-independent bounds for attention perturbations versus dimension-dependent bounds for logit perturbations, and (2) the mechanism through which attention perturbations propagate more gracefully to the output distribution. For notational convenience, we denote conventional contrastive decoding at the logit level as CD, and our proposed contrastive decoding at the attention layer as ACD.

B.1 Perturbation Bounds: Geometric Analysis

We first establish quantitative bounds on perturbation magnitudes in both spaces.

Definition B.1 (Probability Simplex (Boyd and Vandenberghe, 2004)).

The (n−1)(n-1)-dimensional probability simplex is:

Δn−1={𝐩∈ℝn:pi≥0,∑i=1npi=1}.\Delta^{n-1}=\left\{\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:p_{i}\geq 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=1\right\}. (10)
Proposition B.2 (Dimension-Independent Bound for Attention Perturbation).

Let Atc​l​e​a​n,Atn​o​i​s​y∈ΔL−1A_{t}^{clean},A_{t}^{noisy}\in\Delta^{L-1} be attention distributions over sequence length LL. Then:

‖Atc​l​e​a​n−Atn​o​i​s​y‖1≤2,‖Atc​l​e​a​n−Atn​o​i​s​y‖2≤2.\|A_{t}^{clean}-A_{t}^{noisy}\|_{1}\leq 2,\quad\|A_{t}^{clean}-A_{t}^{noisy}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{2}. (11)

These bounds are independent of sequence length LL and model dimension dd.

Proof.

Partition the index set into ℐ+={i:Atc​l​e​a​n​[i]≥Atn​o​i​s​y​[i]}\mathcal{I}^{+}=\{i:A_{t}^{clean}[i]\geq A_{t}^{noisy}[i]\} and ℐ−=ℐ∖ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{-}=\mathcal{I}\setminus\mathcal{I}^{+}. Since both distributions sum to unity:

∑i∈ℐ+(Atc​l​e​a​n​[i]−Atn​o​i​s​y​[i])=∑i∈ℐ−(Atn​o​i​s​y​[i]−Atc​l​e​a​n​[i]).\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}(A_{t}^{clean}[i]-A_{t}^{noisy}[i])=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{-}}(A_{t}^{noisy}[i]-A_{t}^{clean}[i]). (12)

Thus:

‖Atc​l​e​a​n−Atn​o​i​s​y‖1\displaystyle\|A_{t}^{clean}-A_{t}^{noisy}\|_{1} =2​∑i∈ℐ+(Atc​l​e​a​n​[i]−Atn​o​i​s​y​[i])≤2​∑i∈ℐ+Atc​l​e​a​n​[i]≤2.\displaystyle=2\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}(A_{t}^{clean}[i]-A_{t}^{noisy}[i])\leq 2\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}A_{t}^{clean}[i]\leq 2. (13)

For the ℓ2\ell_{2} bound, since |Atc​l​e​a​n​[i]−Atn​o​i​s​y​[i]|≤1|A_{t}^{clean}[i]-A_{t}^{noisy}[i]|\leq 1 for all ii:

‖Atc​l​e​a​n−Atn​o​i​s​y‖22≤maxi⁡|Atc​l​e​a​n​[i]−Atn​o​i​s​y​[i]|⋅‖Atc​l​e​a​n−Atn​o​i​s​y‖1≤1⋅2=2.\|A_{t}^{clean}-A_{t}^{noisy}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\max_{i}|A_{t}^{clean}[i]-A_{t}^{noisy}[i]|\cdot\|A_{t}^{clean}-A_{t}^{noisy}\|_{1}\leq 1\cdot 2=2. (14)

∎

Proposition B.3 (Dimension-Dependent Bound for Logit Perturbation).

In modern Transformer architectures with final LayerNorm (Touvron et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2020), the logit difference satisfies:

‖ztc​l​e​a​n−ztn​o​i​s​y‖2≤2​d⋅‖Whead‖2,\|z_{t}^{clean}-z_{t}^{noisy}\|_{2}\leq 2\sqrt{d}\cdot\|W_{\mathrm{head}}\|_{2}, (15)

where dd is the hidden dimension and Whead∈ℝ|𝒱|×dW_{\mathrm{head}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d} is the language model head.11 1 This assumes standard initialization with normalized variance, under which LayerNorm outputs satisfy ‖h‖2≈d\|h\|_{2}\approx\sqrt{d} (Ba et al., 2016).

Proof.

With LayerNorm applied before the language model head, we have ‖htc​l​e​a​n‖2≈d\|h_{t}^{clean}\|_{2}\approx\sqrt{d} and ‖htn​o​i​s​y‖2≈d\|h_{t}^{noisy}\|_{2}\approx\sqrt{d}. Since z=Whead​hz=W_{\mathrm{head}}h:

‖ztc​l​e​a​n−ztn​o​i​s​y‖2\displaystyle\|z_{t}^{clean}-z_{t}^{noisy}\|_{2} =‖Whead​(htc​l​e​a​n−htn​o​i​s​y)‖2≤‖Whead‖2⋅‖htc​l​e​a​n−htn​o​i​s​y‖2.\displaystyle=\|W_{\mathrm{head}}(h_{t}^{clean}-h_{t}^{noisy})\|_{2}\leq\|W_{\mathrm{head}}\|_{2}\cdot\|h_{t}^{clean}-h_{t}^{noisy}\|_{2}. (16)

By triangle inequality, ‖htc​l​e​a​n−htn​o​i​s​y‖2≤‖htc​l​e​a​n‖2+‖htn​o​i​s​y‖2≤2​d\|h_{t}^{clean}-h_{t}^{noisy}\|_{2}\leq\|h_{t}^{clean}\|_{2}+\|h_{t}^{noisy}\|_{2}\leq 2\sqrt{d}. ∎

Remark B.4 (Scaling Comparison).

The critical distinction lies in the scaling behavior:

  • •

    Attention perturbation: O⁡(1)O(1), bounded by 2\sqrt{2} regardless of model scale.

  • •

    Logit perturbation: O⁡(d⋅‖Whead‖2)O(\sqrt{d}\cdot\|W_{\mathrm{head}}\|_{2}), grows with model dimension.

For LLaVA-1.5-7B with d=4096d=4096 and typical ‖Whead‖2≈10\|W_{\mathrm{head}}\|_{2}\approx 10, the logit perturbation bound is ≈1280\approx 1280, approximately three orders of magnitude larger than the attention bound of 2≈1.41\sqrt{2}\approx 1.41.

B.2 Propagation Mechanism Analysis

Beyond magnitude bounds, the mechanism through which perturbations affect outputs differs fundamentally between CD and ACD.

Definition B.5 (Contrastive Perturbation Operators).

Define the perturbation operators for CD and ACD:

𝒫CD​(zc​l​e​a​n,zn​o​i​s​y,α)\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{CD}}(z^{clean},z^{noisy};\alpha) =(1+α)​zc​l​e​a​n−α​zn​o​i​s​y,\displaystyle=(1+\alpha)z^{clean}-\alpha z^{noisy}, (17)
𝒫ACD​(Ac​l​e​a​n,An​o​i​s​y,α)\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{ACD}}(A^{clean},A^{noisy};\alpha) =(1+α)​Ac​l​e​a​n−α⁡(An​o​i​s​y⊙M),\displaystyle=(1+\alpha)A^{clean}-\alpha(A^{noisy}\odot M), (18)

where MM is the adaptive mask from Section 3.3.

Theorem B.6 (Propagation Path Length).

Let Φ:A(l)↦z\Phi:A^{(l)}\mapsto z denote the forward computation from attention at layer ll to final logits. The computational paths differ qualitatively:

CD: z→𝒫CDzC​D→softmaxpC​D,\displaystyle z\xrightarrow{\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{CD}}}z^{CD}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{softmax}}p^{CD}, (19)
ACD: A(l)→𝒫ACDAA​C​D→Value Agg.→Proj.→LN→FFN→⋯→HeadzA​C​D→softmaxpA​C​D.\displaystyle A^{(l)}\xrightarrow{\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{ACD}}}A^{ACD}\xrightarrow{\text{Value Agg.}}\xrightarrow{\text{Proj.}}\xrightarrow{\text{LN}}\xrightarrow{\text{FFN}}\xrightarrow{\cdots}\xrightarrow{\text{Head}}z^{ACD}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{softmax}}p^{ACD}. (20)

CD applies perturbation directly before softmax (path length 1), while ACD’s perturbation traverses (N−l+1)(N-l+1) layers before affecting output probabilities.

The extended propagation path in ACD induces two stabilizing effects:

(1) Subspace Confinement via Value Aggregation. The attention output is computed as O=A​VO=AV where V∈ℝL×dvV\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_{v}} is the value matrix. Consequently, the output lies in colspan⁡(V⊤)\mathrm{colspan}(V^{\top}), the column space of V⊤V^{\top}. When attention is perturbed by Δ​A=AA​C​D−Ac​l​e​a​n\Delta A=A^{ACD}-A^{clean}, the resulting hidden state perturbation satisfies:

Δ​h(l)=Δ​A⋅V∈colspan⁡(V⊤).\Delta h^{(l)}=\Delta A\cdot V\in\mathrm{colspan}(V^{\top}). (21)
Proposition B.7 (Low-Rank Confinement).

Let rank⁡(V)=r≤min⁡(L,dv)\mathrm{rank}(V)=r\leq\min(L,d_{v}). Then the attention-induced perturbation Δ​h(l)\Delta h^{(l)} is confined to an rr-dimensional subspace of ℝdv\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}, regardless of the perturbation Δ​A\Delta A.

Proof.

Since Δ​h(l)=Δ​A⋅V\Delta h^{(l)}=\Delta A\cdot V and VV has rank rr, we have Δ​h(l)∈colspan⁡(V⊤)\Delta h^{(l)}\in\mathrm{colspan}(V^{\top}), which has dimension exactly rr. The perturbation cannot escape this subspace regardless of the choice of Δ​A∈ℝ1×L\Delta A\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times L}. ∎

In deep layers where contextualized representations converge, VV often exhibits approximate low-rank structure (Wang et al., 2020), further constraining the effective dimensionality of attention perturbations. This geometric confinement has no analogue in logit-level CD, where perturbations can span the full |𝒱||\mathcal{V}|-dimensional vocabulary space.

(2) LayerNorm Stabilization. While LayerNorm is not strictly contractive due to the learned scale parameter (Xu et al., 2019), it provides directional stabilization: for input xx with perturbation Δ​x\Delta x, the first-order approximation yields:

LayerNorm⁡(x+Δ​x)≈LayerNorm⁡(x)+γσx​Πx⟂​(Δ​x),\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x+\Delta x)\approx\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x)+\frac{\gamma}{\sigma_{x}}\Pi_{x}^{\perp}(\Delta x), (22)

where σx\sigma_{x} is the standard deviation of xx, γ\gamma is the learned scale, and Πx⟂\Pi_{x}^{\perp} projects onto the subspace orthogonal to both xx and the all-ones vector. This projection removes two degrees of freedom from Δ​x\Delta x, effectively constraining perturbations to a (d−2)(d-2)-dimensional subspace at each layer (Ba et al., 2016).

B.3 Softmax Sensitivity and Rank Stability

The most critical distinction concerns how perturbations affect the output probability distribution through the softmax function.

Lemma B.8 (Softmax Lipschitz Property (Gao and Pavel, 2017)).

For the softmax function σ:ℝn→Δn−1\sigma:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\Delta^{n-1}, the following Lipschitz bound holds:

‖σ⁡(z)−σ⁡(z′)‖2≤‖z−z′‖2.\|\sigma(z)-\sigma(z^{\prime})\|_{2}\leq\|z-z^{\prime}\|_{2}. (23)

That is, softmax is 1-Lipschitz with respect to the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm.

Lemma B.9 (Total Variation via ℓ2\ell_{2} Bound).

For probability distributions p,p′∈Δn−1p,p^{\prime}\in\Delta^{n-1}, the total variation distance satisfies:

TV⁡(p,p′)=12​‖p−p′‖1≤n2​‖p−p′‖2.\mathrm{TV}(p,p^{\prime})=\frac{1}{2}\|p-p^{\prime}\|_{1}\leq\frac{\sqrt{n}}{2}\|p-p^{\prime}\|_{2}. (24)
Proof.

By definition, TV⁡(p,p′)=12​‖p−p′‖1\mathrm{TV}(p,p^{\prime})=\frac{1}{2}\|p-p^{\prime}\|_{1}. Applying the norm inequality ‖x‖1≤n​‖x‖2\|x\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{n}\|x\|_{2} for x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} yields the result. ∎

Theorem B.10 (Rank Inversion Condition in Logit-Level CD).

Consider two tokens i,ji,j with zic​l​e​a​n>zjc​l​e​a​nz_{i}^{clean}>z_{j}^{clean} (token ii preferred under clean input). Under CD with strength α\alpha, rank inversion (ziC​D<zjC​Dz_{i}^{CD}<z_{j}^{CD}) occurs if and only if:

zin​o​i​s​y−zjn​o​i​s​y>1+αα​(zic​l​e​a​n−zjc​l​e​a​n).z_{i}^{noisy}-z_{j}^{noisy}>\frac{1+\alpha}{\alpha}(z_{i}^{clean}-z_{j}^{clean}). (25)
Proof.

From zC​D=(1+α)​zc​l​e​a​n−α​zn​o​i​s​yz^{CD}=(1+\alpha)z^{clean}-\alpha z^{noisy}:

ziC​D<zjC​D\displaystyle z_{i}^{CD}<z_{j}^{CD} ⇔(1+α)​(zic​l​e​a​n−zjc​l​e​a​n)<α⁡(zin​o​i​s​y−zjn​o​i​s​y)\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow(1+\alpha)(z_{i}^{clean}-z_{j}^{clean})<\alpha(z_{i}^{noisy}-z_{j}^{noisy}) (26)
⇔zin​o​i​s​y−zjn​o​i​s​y>1+αα​(zic​l​e​a​n−zjc​l​e​a​n).\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow z_{i}^{noisy}-z_{j}^{noisy}>\frac{1+\alpha}{\alpha}(z_{i}^{clean}-z_{j}^{clean}). (27)

∎

Corollary B.11 (Invalid Token Amplification).

For α=1\alpha=1, rank inversion occurs when the noisy preference margin exceeds twice the clean preference margin. As α→∞\alpha\to\infty, the threshold 1+αα→1\frac{1+\alpha}{\alpha}\to 1, making rank inversions increasingly likely for any token pair where the noisy and clean preferences disagree.

Remark B.12 (Why ACD Avoids Rank Inversion).

ACD perturbations at the attention level do not directly modify logit differences. The mapping Φ:A↦z\Phi:A\mapsto z is a complex nonlinear composition involving value aggregation (which confines perturbations to a subspace per Proposition B.7), projections, LayerNorms (which provide directional stabilization), and FFNs. Crucially, there exists no simple linear relationship between attention magnitude changes and token logit changes—a token’s logit depends on the full sequence context processed through multiple layers, not on any single attention weight. This decoupling between attention perturbations and token rankings provides natural robustness against rank inversion.

B.4 Main Result: Smoothness Guarantee

Theorem B.13 (Smoothness of ACD Output Distribution).

Let pv​a​n​i​l​l​ap^{vanilla}, pC​Dp^{CD}, pA​C​D∈Δ|𝒱|−1p^{ACD}\in\Delta^{|\mathcal{V}|-1} denote the output token distributions under vanilla decoding, logit-level CD, and attention-level ACD, respectively. Define the distribution shifts:

ΔCD=TV⁡(pC​D,pv​a​n​i​l​l​a),ΔACD=TV⁡(pA​C​D,pv​a​n​i​l​l​a).\Delta_{\mathrm{CD}}=\mathrm{TV}(p^{CD},p^{vanilla}),\quad\Delta_{\mathrm{ACD}}=\mathrm{TV}(p^{ACD},p^{vanilla}). (28)

Then:

(I) [Direct Bound for CD] Combining Lemmas B.8 and B.9:

ΔCD\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{CD}} =12​‖pC​D−pv​a​n​i​l​l​a‖1≤|𝒱|2​‖pC​D−pv​a​n​i​l​l​a‖2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\|p^{CD}-p^{vanilla}\|_{1}\leq\frac{\sqrt{|\mathcal{V}|}}{2}\|p^{CD}-p^{vanilla}\|_{2}
≤|𝒱|2​‖zC​D−zc​l​e​a​n‖2=α​|𝒱|2​‖zc​l​e​a​n−zn​o​i​s​y‖2\displaystyle\leq\frac{\sqrt{|\mathcal{V}|}}{2}\|z^{CD}-z^{clean}\|_{2}=\frac{\alpha\sqrt{|\mathcal{V}|}}{2}\|z^{clean}-z^{noisy}\|_{2}
≤α​|𝒱|⋅d⋅‖Whead‖2=O⁡(α​d⋅|𝒱|),\displaystyle\leq\alpha\sqrt{|\mathcal{V}|}\cdot\sqrt{d}\cdot\|W_{\mathrm{head}}\|_{2}=O(\alpha\sqrt{d\cdot|\mathcal{V}|}), (29)

where the final inequality applies Proposition B.3.

(II) [Structural Bound for ACD] The ACD perturbation propagates through Φ\Phi:

ΔACD≤|𝒱|2​‖zA​C​D−zc​l​e​a​n‖2=|𝒱|2​‖Φ⁡(AA​C​D)−Φ⁡(Ac​l​e​a​n)‖2.\Delta_{\mathrm{ACD}}\leq\frac{\sqrt{|\mathcal{V}|}}{2}\|z^{ACD}-z^{clean}\|_{2}=\frac{\sqrt{|\mathcal{V}|}}{2}\|\Phi(A^{ACD})-\Phi(A^{clean})\|_{2}. (30)

While Φ\Phi involves residual connections that preclude global contraction guarantees, the input perturbation satisfies the dimension-independent bound ‖AA​C​D−Ac​l​e​a​n‖2≤α​2\|A^{ACD}-A^{clean}\|_{2}\leq\alpha\sqrt{2} (Proposition B.2), and propagation through value aggregation confines perturbations to a low-rank subspace (Proposition B.7). Combined with LayerNorm stabilization, these mechanisms yield empirically observed smoothness ΔACD≪ΔCD\Delta_{\mathrm{ACD}}\ll\Delta_{\mathrm{CD}}, validated in Section C.

Corollary B.14 (Elimination of Penalty Mechanisms).

The bounded attention perturbation (Proposition B.2) combined with the subspace confinement (Proposition B.7) and indirect propagation mechanism (Theorem B.6) ensures that ACD does not cause severe rank inversions (Theorem B.10). Consequently, the penalty mechanism in Equation 5—designed to filter invalid tokens arising from rank inversions—becomes unnecessary under ACD, enabling simpler deployment without hyperparameter tuning for β\beta.

Corollary B.15 (Robustness to Contrastive Strength).

Since ‖AA​C​D−Ac​l​e​a​n‖2≤α​2\|A^{ACD}-A^{clean}\|_{2}\leq\alpha\sqrt{2} scales linearly with α\alpha with a small, dimension-independent coefficient (2≈1.41\sqrt{2}\approx 1.41), ACD maintains stable performance across varying α\alpha values. In contrast, CD’s perturbation α​‖zc​l​e​a​n−zn​o​i​s​y‖2\alpha\|z^{clean}-z^{noisy}\|_{2} has a dimension-dependent coefficient that can reach O⁡(d)O(\sqrt{d}), amplifying instability at high α\alpha. This analysis is consistent with empirical observations in Figure 6.

Remark B.16 (Information-Geometric Perspective).

The probability simplex Δn−1\Delta^{n-1} equipped with the Fisher-Rao metric exhibits curvature that increases near boundaries where some pi→0p_{i}\to 0. This intrinsic geometry implicitly penalizes perturbations that push attention toward extreme values, providing geometric regularization absent in the flat Euclidean structure of logit space.

Appendix C Empirical Validation of Distribution Smoothness and Decoding Coherence

Our theoretical analysis in Section B establishes that attention-level contrastive operations yield smoother output distributions than logit-level interventions, owing to dimension-independent perturbation bounds (Proposition B.2), low-rank subspace confinement (Proposition B.7), and the extended propagation path through stabilizing architectural components (Theorem B.6). In this section, we provide comprehensive empirical evidence corroborating these theoretical predictions.

C.1 Experimental Protocol

We evaluate the distributional smoothness of VCD (logit-level contrastive decoding) and VCD+ACD (attention-level contrastive decoding applied on top of VCD) using LLaVA-1.5-7B (Liu et al., 2023b) on the CHAIR benchmark (Yue et al., 2024). We sample 500 images and generate captions with a maximum token length of 128. At each decoding step tt, we record the output probability distribution and compute two complementary divergence measures relative to the vanilla (unperturbed) decoding distribution ptvanillap_{t}^{\text{vanilla}}:

  • •

    Total Variation (TV) Distance: TV⁡(pt,ptvanilla)=12​‖pt−ptvanilla‖1\mathrm{TV}(p_{t},p_{t}^{\text{vanilla}})=\frac{1}{2}\|p_{t}-p_{t}^{\text{vanilla}}\|_{1}, which directly measures the maximum difference in event probabilities and corresponds to the theoretical bounds in Theorem B.13.

  • •

    KL Divergence: DKL(ptvanilla∥pt)=∑iptvanilla(i)logptvanilla​(i)pt​(i)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{t}^{\text{vanilla}}\|p_{t})=\sum_{i}p_{t}^{\text{vanilla}}(i)\log\frac{p_{t}^{\text{vanilla}}(i)}{p_{t}(i)}, which captures information-theoretic distortion and is particularly sensitive to probability mass assigned to unlikely tokens.

We visualize the results through four complementary perspectives: (1) aggregate box plots summarizing overall distributional statistics, (2) violin plots revealing the full density shape of divergence values, and (3,4) step-wise trajectory plots with ±1\pm 1 standard deviation bands illustrating temporal dynamics across the decoding process.

C.2 Results and Analysis

Overall Distribution Shift (TV Distance).

As shown in Figures 4(a) and 4(b), VCD+ACD achieves a dramatic reduction of 79.9% in mean TV distance compared to VCD (μ=0.131\mu=0.131 vs. μ=0.653\mu=0.653). The box plot reveals that VCD’s interquartile range (IQR) spans approximately [0.49,0.87][0.49,0.87] with the median at 0.720.72, indicating that logit-level subtraction pervasively distorts the output distribution—over half of all decoding steps exhibit a TV distance exceeding 0.70.7, signifying that the top-ranked token under VCD frequently differs from that of vanilla decoding. In stark contrast, VCD+ACD’s IQR is compressed to approximately [0.04,0.19][0.04,0.19] with a median of 0.110.11, confirming that attention-level perturbations preserve the overall distributional structure with minimal deviation.

The violin plot further elucidates the density profile: VCD’s distribution mass concentrates in the high-divergence regime (0.60.6–1.01.0) with a pronounced mode near 1.01.0—the theoretical maximum of TV distance—indicating frequent near-complete redistribution of probability mass. Conversely, VCD+ACD exhibits a sharply peaked distribution concentrated near zero, with only a thin tail extending beyond 0.40.4. This empirical observation directly validates Theorem B.13: the dimension-independent bound on attention perturbations (‖AA​C​D−Ac​l​e​a​n‖2≤α​2\|A^{ACD}-A^{clean}\|_{2}\leq\alpha\sqrt{2}) combined with low-rank confinement and LayerNorm stabilization yields substantially smaller distributional shifts compared to the dimension-dependent logit perturbation bound of O⁡(α​d⋅|𝒱|)O(\alpha\sqrt{d\cdot|\mathcal{V}|}).

Information-Theoretic Distortion (KL Divergence).

Figures 4(c) and 4(d) present the KL divergence analysis. VCD+ACD reduces mean KL divergence by 10.7% (μ=1.927\mu=1.927 vs. μ=2.157\mu=2.157). While this relative reduction appears modest compared to the TV distance improvement, two critical observations merit emphasis. First, VCD exhibits substantially heavier tails: the box plot shows numerous outliers exceeding 1010 nats, with extreme values reaching 21.121.1 nats, whereas VCD+ACD’s outliers are capped at approximately 11.211.2 nats. The violin plot corroborates this finding—VCD’s density exhibits a visible secondary mode in the 1212–1818 range, corresponding to decoding steps where logit-level subtraction catastrophically distorts the probability distribution. Such extreme KL values indicate that VCD occasionally assigns near-zero probability to tokens favored by vanilla decoding, a pathological behavior consistent with the rank inversion phenomenon characterized in Theorem B.10. Second, VCD+ACD’s IQR is more compact (approximately [0.5,3.0][0.5,3.0] vs. [0.8,3.5][0.8,3.5]), reflecting more predictable and controlled distributional modifications.

The asymmetry between the TV and KL improvements is theoretically expected: KL divergence is dominated by tail behavior (log⁡pq\log\frac{p}{q} diverges as q→0q\to 0), and both methods occasionally produce small probability perturbations that inflate KL values. However, TV distance, which corresponds to the ℓ1\ell_{1} norm of the probability difference, is more faithful to the overall distributional shape—precisely the quantity bounded by our theoretical analysis.

Temporal Dynamics Across Decoding Steps.

The step-wise trajectory plots (Figures 4(e) and 4(f)) reveal the temporal coherence of both methods throughout the autoregressive generation process.

For TV distance (Figure 4(e)), VCD exhibits consistently high distortion (0.50.5–0.70.7) with a large standard deviation band spanning nearly the entire [0,1][0,1] range, indicating highly variable and unpredictable distributional shifts across both time steps and samples. Notably, VCD’s mean TV distance increases slightly over time (from ∼\sim0.5 at step 10 to ∼\sim0.7 at step 128), suggesting that distributional perturbations accumulate as the generated sequence grows longer—a consequence of error propagation in autoregressive decoding where each distorted token conditions subsequent generation. In contrast, VCD+ACD maintains remarkably stable TV distances (0.10.1–0.20.2) with a narrow standard deviation band throughout the entire decoding horizon. This temporal stability empirically validates Corollary B.15: since attention perturbations are bounded by a dimension-independent constant at every layer and every step, the resulting output distribution remains consistently close to the vanilla distribution regardless of sequence length.

For KL divergence (Figure 4(f)), both methods exhibit an initial transient phase (steps 1–5) with elevated divergence, attributable to the high uncertainty in early-stage token prediction where the context window is minimal. After this transient, VCD+ACD converges to a lower and more stable trajectory (∼\sim1.5–2.0 nats) compared to VCD (∼\sim2.0–2.5 nats). Crucially, VCD’s standard deviation band remains substantially wider throughout, confirming that logit-level subtraction introduces heterogeneous perturbation magnitudes that vary unpredictably across decoding steps—precisely the instability predicted by the dimension-dependent bound in Proposition B.3.

Summary.

The empirical results across all six diagnostic visualizations converge on a consistent conclusion: ACD produces fundamentally smoother, more coherent, and more temporally stable output distributions than logit-level contrastive decoding. The 79.9% reduction in TV distance validates our theoretical prediction that attention-level operations, constrained by dimension-independent bounds and low-rank subspace confinement, preserve the model’s intrinsic generation distribution far more faithfully than logit-level interventions. The temporal trajectory analysis further demonstrates that this smoothness advantage is not merely an aggregate statistical artifact but persists consistently across every decoding step, ensuring coherent and stable generation throughout the entire output sequence. These findings provide strong empirical support for Theorem B.13 and Corollary B.14, substantiating that ACD’s architectural design eliminates the need for auxiliary penalty mechanisms while maintaining superior distributional fidelity.

Appendix D Robustness to Contrastive Strength α\alpha

Our theoretical analysis (Corollary B.15) predicts that ACD exhibits superior robustness to the contrastive strength hyperparameter α\alpha due to its dimension-independent perturbation bound. We empirically validate this prediction by conducting ablation studies on both VCD and VCD+ACD using LLaVA-1.5-7B on the CHAIR benchmark.

Results.

Figure 5 presents performance trajectories across α\alpha values. VCD achieves optimal performance at α=1.0\alpha=1.0 but degrades substantially at non-optimal values—at α=1.5\alpha=1.5, CHAIRi increases by 50% (from 16.2 to 24.3). In contrast, VCD+ACD maintains remarkably stable performance across its entire evaluated range (α∈[0.05,0.25]\alpha\in[0.05,0.25]), with CHAIRi varying by only 2.2 points.

Figure 6 normalizes α\alpha to each method’s optimum for direct comparison. VCD exhibits steep degradation curves, with performance declining rapidly as α\alpha deviates from optimal. VCD+ACD displays a nearly flat response, with degradation remaining below 5% even at boundary values. Quantitatively, VCD+ACD achieves approximately 78% lower standard deviation across all metrics compared to VCD.

This contrast directly reflects the theoretical distinction: VCD’s perturbation scales as O⁡(α​d)O(\alpha\sqrt{d}) with a large dimension-dependent coefficient, while ACD’s perturbation scales as O⁡(α)O(\alpha) with coefficient 2≈1.41\sqrt{2}\approx 1.41. The dimension-independent bound acts as a natural regularizer, ensuring stable performance regardless of α\alpha selection.

Appendix E Decoding Procedure

The specific algorithm is as follows in Algorithm 1.

During practical decoding, the ACD method maintains dual attention caches: an original cache and a hallucination cache. At each decoding step, ACD computes attention distributions for both original and hallucination-inducing inputs, subsequently applying the ASS strategy to identify and suppress attention allocations that amplify important semantic information potentially conducive to hallucination generation. This fine-grained intervention at the attention layer enables the model to maintain linguistic coherence and diversity while effectively mitigating hallucinations. In contrast to traditional CD methods, ACD eliminates the necessity for 𝒱head\mathcal{V}_{\text{head}} penalty mechanisms as formulated in Equation 5 to filter low-probability tokens, as its attention-layer intervention inherently prevents invalid token generation. This characteristic allows ACD to reduce hallucinations while preserving content quality and diversity. The fundamental advantage of ACD lies in its exploitation of the inherent smoothness and structural continuity of the Transformer attention mechanism, enabling the model to precisely localize and suppress hallucination sources while maintaining generation quality. This approach provides a more reliable decoding solution for practical LVLM applications, effectively balancing hallucination mitigation with output quality preservation.

Appendix F Layer-wise Propagation and Semantic Alignment

We analyze how the perturbation introduced in the noisy stream propagates through the transformer layers and establish that the resulting divergence remains bounded—providing the theoretical foundation for ACD’s contrastive mechanism.

F.1 Residual Stream Dynamics

Consider a transformer with LL layers. Let 𝐡l(c)\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)} and 𝐡l(n)\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)} denote the hidden states at layer ll for the clean and noisy streams, respectively. The residual update rule gives:

𝐡l+1(c)=𝐡l(c)+fl​(𝐡l(c)),𝐡l+1(n)=𝐡l(n)+fl​(𝐡l(n)),\mathbf{h}_{l+1}^{(c)}=\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)}+f_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)}),\quad\mathbf{h}_{l+1}^{(n)}=\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)}+f_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)}), (31)

where fl​(⋅)f_{l}(\cdot) denotes the combined self-attention and feed-forward transformation at layer ll. Define the inter-stream divergence as 𝜹l=𝐡l(c)−𝐡l(n)\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l}=\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)}-\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)}. Its recurrence is:

𝜹l+1=𝜹l+[fl​(𝐡l(c))−fl​(𝐡l(n))].\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l+1}=\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l}+\big[f_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)})-f_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)})\big]. (32)
Proposition F.1 (Bounded Cumulative Divergence).

Assume each layer transformation flf_{l} is Lipschitz continuous with constant Kl<1K_{l}<1. Then the divergence satisfies:

‖𝜹l+1‖≤‖𝜹l‖+Kl​‖𝜹l‖=(1+Kl)​‖𝜹l‖.\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l+1}\|\leq\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l}\|+K_{l}\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l}\|=(1+K_{l})\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l}\|. (33)

Unrolling through all layers yields:

‖𝜹L‖≤‖𝜹0‖​∏l=0L−1(1+Kl).\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{L}\|\leq\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{0}\|\prod_{l=0}^{L-1}(1+K_{l}). (34)

When Kl≪1K_{l}\ll 1 (as enforced by LayerNorm and residual scaling), ∏l(1+Kl)≈exp⁡(∑lKl)\prod_{l}(1+K_{l})\approx\exp\!\big(\sum_{l}K_{l}\big), so the divergence grows at most exponentially in the sum of Lipschitz constants rather than unboundedly.

In practice, the pre-trained LLM satisfies a stronger condition. Denoting the cosine similarity sl=cos⁡(𝐡l(c),𝐡l(n))s_{l}=\cos(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)},\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)}), we can decompose the per-layer similarity change as:

sl+1=⟨𝐡l(c)+fl​(𝐡l(c)),𝐡l(n)+fl​(𝐡l(n))⟩‖𝐡l(c)+fl​(𝐡l(c))‖⋅‖𝐡l(n)+fl​(𝐡l(n))‖.s_{l+1}=\frac{\langle\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)}+f_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)}),\;\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)}+f_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)})\rangle}{\|\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)}+f_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)})\|\;\cdot\;\|\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)}+f_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)})\|}. (35)

Expanding the numerator:

⟨𝐡l+1(c),𝐡l+1(n)⟩\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{h}_{l+1}^{(c)},\mathbf{h}_{l+1}^{(n)}\rangle =⟨𝐡l(c),𝐡l(n)⟩+⟨𝐡l(c),fl​(𝐡l(n))⟩\displaystyle=\langle\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)},\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)}\rangle+\langle\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)},f_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)})\rangle (36)
+⟨fl​(𝐡l(c)),𝐡l(n)⟩+⟨fl​(𝐡l(c)),fl​(𝐡l(n))⟩.\displaystyle+\langle f_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)}),\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)}\rangle+\langle f_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)}),f_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)})\rangle.

The residual term ⟨𝐡l(c),𝐡l(n)⟩\langle\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(c)},\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(n)}\rangle dominates the cross terms when ‖fl‖≪‖𝐡l‖\|f_{l}\|\ll\|\mathbf{h}_{l}\|, which prevents sls_{l} from collapsing to zero even across many layers. This explains the bounded, non-monotonic similarity profile observed empirically.

Corollary F.2 (Modality-Dependent Divergence).

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} and 𝒱\mathcal{V} denote the index sets of text and visual tokens. Since the two streams share identical text inputs but differ in visual inputs, the initial divergence satisfies ‖𝛅0(𝒯)‖=0\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{0}^{(\mathcal{T})}\|=0 and ‖𝛅0(𝒱)‖>0\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{0}^{(\mathcal{V})}\|>0. By Proposition F.1, for all layers ll:

𝔼⁡[sl(𝒯)]>𝔼⁡[sl(𝒱)],\mathbb{E}\big[s_{l}^{(\mathcal{T})}\big]\;>\;\mathbb{E}\big[s_{l}^{(\mathcal{V})}\big], (37)

i.e., text tokens consistently maintain higher inter-stream similarity than visual tokens. The gap Δl=𝔼⁡[sl(𝒯)]−𝔼⁡[sl(𝒱)]\Delta_{l}=\mathbb{E}[s_{l}^{(\mathcal{T})}]-\mathbb{E}[s_{l}^{(\mathcal{V})}] quantifies the modality-dependent perturbation signal that ACD exploits.

F.2 Empirical Validation

We measure per-layer cosine similarity between clean and noisy hidden states on 100 randomly sampled CHAIR instances (noise step T=800T{=}800). Figure 7 reports the mean and standard deviation across samples.

Three findings emerge from the empirical results:

(1) Bounded, non-monotonic divergence. The overall similarity does not decay monotonically. It reaches a minimum of 0.590.59 around layer 18 before recovering in deeper layers, confirming Proposition F.1—residual connections prevent unbounded divergence accumulation. Across all 32 layers, similarity remains above 0.590.59, indicating that the two streams never become semantically orthogonal.

(2) Modality gap. Text tokens maintain a mean similarity of 0.71±0.040.71\pm 0.04, while visual tokens show 0.62±0.040.62\pm 0.04, yielding a consistent gap Δ≈0.09\Delta\approx 0.09 (Corollary F.2). This gap arises because text tokens receive identical embeddings in both streams, whereas visual token representations are directly perturbed. The gap persists across all layers, providing a stable contrastive signal.

(3) Informative divergence regime. The moderate similarity range (0.590.59–0.710.71) is neither too high nor too low. If streams were near-identical (sl>0.95s_{l}>0.95), ACD would have no contrastive signal to exploit; if they were orthogonal (sl≈0s_{l}\approx 0), the noisy stream would carry no semantically meaningful structure. The observed regime provides sufficient contrast to identify hallucination-prone attention patterns while preserving the shared semantic backbone for valid reasoning. This validates our design choice of noise step T=800T{=}800, which places the perturbation in this informative divergence regime.

Appendix G More RELATED WORK

G.1 Large Vision-Language Models

Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs)(Liu et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2023c; Liu et al., 2024a; Zhu et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023a; Driess et al., 2023; Achiam et al., 2023; Chowdhery et al., 2023; Alayrac et al., 2022) have emerged as a pivotal research direction, effectively bridging computer vision and natural language processing paradigms. These models demonstrate exceptional capabilities across diverse multimodal tasks, including image captioning(Lin et al., 2014; Li et al., 2023a), visual question answering (VQA)(Liu et al., 2023c; Liu et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2024a; Hudson and Manning, 2019), and sophisticated multimodal reasoning(Lu et al., 2022; Alayrac et al., 2022; Achiam et al., 2023). Modern LVLM architectures typically integrate visual encoders (Tong et al., 2024) with feature projection modules (Liu et al., 2023c; Liu et al., 2024a; Zhu et al., 2023) that interface with large language models (LLMs) (Radford et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020; Raffel et al., 2020; Chowdhery et al., 2023; Thoppilan et al., 2022; Achiam et al., 2023), creating a unified embedding space where visual and textual representations converge to enable sophisticated cross-modal understanding. Despite significant advances in LVLMs, hallucination phenomena (Li et al., 2023c; Fu et al., 2023b; Yue et al., 2024)—wherein models generate content fundamentally inconsistent with visual inputs—remain a critical limitation. This work addresses the challenge of hallucination mitigation in contemporary LVLMs, aiming to enhance their reliability and expand their applicability across diverse domains.

G.2 Broader Context

Adaptive feature recalibration and robust representation learning are fundamental challenges in visual perception. A growing body of work addresses representational fidelity under distributional shift (Li et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026b; Tao et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2024a; Deng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025d), developing adaptive strategies to preserve semantically meaningful signals amid noisy or out-of-distribution inputs. Balancing competing objectives without sacrificing output quality has also attracted considerable attention (Sun et al., 2025b; Sun et al., 2025a). In the context of cross-modal understanding, selective and structure-preserving alignment between heterogeneous representations remains an active research direction (Cheng et al., 2025b; Cheng et al., 2025a; Cheng et al., 2025c; Cheng et al., 2026d; Cheng et al., 2026c; Cheng et al., 2026b; Cheng et al., 2026a; Cheng, 2026; Cheng et al., 2024), as does training-free adaptive inference for vision-language models (Chen et al., 2025b).

Appendix H Benchmarks and Evaluation Metric Details

This section delineates the comprehensive evaluation framework employed in our experimental analysis, encompassing four distinct benchmark datasets and their corresponding evaluation protocols designed to systematically assess hallucination mitigation efficacy across varied visual reasoning paradigms.

H.1 CHAIR

CHAIR (Yue et al., 2024) (Caption Hallucination Assessment with Image Relevance) quantifies object hallucination severity in generated image descriptions. Unlike conventional metrics that evaluate image descriptions through lexical or syntactic similarity, CHAIR directly leverages image annotation metadata to identify hallucination instances, thereby measuring semantic consistency between generated descriptions and actual visual content with greater precision. The CHAIR framework comprises two complementary metrics:

  • •

    C​H​A​I​RsCHAIR_{s} (sentence-level): Measures the proportion of generated sentences containing at least one hallucinated object

  • •

    C​H​A​I​RiCHAIR_{i} (instance-level): Quantifies the ratio of hallucinated object mentions to total object mentions across all generated descriptions

Additionally, recall serves as a complementary metric to evaluate semantic comprehensiveness, measuring the proportion of ground-truth objects successfully captured in the generated descriptions. This methodological approach circumvents potential biases inherent in purely linguistic matching techniques, offering enhanced sensitivity in hallucination detection while revealing semantic fidelity deficiencies that might remain undetected through traditional evaluation frameworks.

C​H​A​I​Rs=|{Captions with hallucinated objects}||{All captions}|CHAIR_{s}=\frac{|\{\text{Captions with hallucinated objects}\}|}{|\{\text{All captions}\}|} (38)
C​H​A​I​Ri=|{Hallucinated objects}||{All mentioned objects}|CHAIR_{i}=\frac{|\{\text{Hallucinated objects}\}|}{|\{\text{All mentioned objects}\}|} (39)
R​e​c​a​l​l=|{Accurate objects}||{Ground-truth objects}|Recall=\frac{|\{\text{Accurate objects}\}|}{|\{\text{Ground-truth objects}\}|} (40)

H.2 LLaVA-Bench (In-the-Wild)

LLaVA-Bench (In-the-Wild) (Liu et al., 2023b) encompasses diverse challenging visual scenarios including indoor/outdoor environments, internet memes, paintings, sketches, and various artistic or abstract imagery typically underrepresented in standard training distributions. This benchmark deliberately introduces distributional shifts to assess model generalization capabilities across challenging visual contexts. The dataset comprises 24 distinct images with 60 corresponding questions, each image accompanied by meticulously crafted comprehensive descriptions and multiple targeted questions. Following an instruction-following evaluation paradigm, models receive visual inputs paired with natural language instructions requiring appropriate responses. The assessment protocol incorporates questions spanning fundamental visual comprehension to complex inferential reasoning. Given the absence of standardized ground truth evaluations, we employ GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025), currently the most advanced Large Vision-Language Model available, as an automatic evaluator for generated descriptions. Through carefully engineered prompting (illustrated in Figure 13), the evaluation assesses model outputs along two critical dimensions: (1) Accuracy—measuring semantic consistency between generated descriptions and visual content; and (2) Detailedness—quantifying the richness and comprehensiveness of visual details captured in model-generated descriptions. This automated evaluation methodology enables consistent assessment of model performance across challenging out-of-distribution visual scenarios.

H.3 POPE

POPE (Li et al., 2023c) (Polling-based Object Presence Evaluation) formalizes the assessment of object hallucination as a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with yes/no questions regarding object presence in images. Each evaluation sample consists of a triplet containing an image, corresponding question, and ground-truth answer. The framework constructs both positive and negative question instances with varying difficulty levels through three distinct sampling strategies: Random sampling—selecting arbitrarily from objects absent in the image; Popular sampling—selecting the top l2\tfrac{l}{2} most frequent objects across the dataset that are absent from the current image; and Adversarial sampling—selecting the top kk absent objects ranked by co-occurrence frequency with objects present in the image. Our POPE evaluation dataset incorporates over 20,000 question-answer pairs constructed from MSCOCO (Lin et al., 2014), A-OKVQA (Schwenk et al., 2022), and GQA (Hudson and Manning, 2019) datasets. Within the POPE evaluation framework, model responses are constrained to binary ”Yes” or ”No” outputs, effectively transforming object hallucination detection into a standard binary classification problem. Consequently, we employ established classification metrics—Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score—to quantitatively assess model performance. These metrics are formally defined as:

Accuracy=T​P+T​NT​P+T​N+F​P+F​N,\text{Accuracy}=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}, (41)
Precision=T​PT​P+F​P,\text{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}, (42)
Recall=T​PT​P+F​N,\text{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}, (43)
F1-score=2⋅Precision⋅RecallPrecision+Recall,\text{F1-score}=\frac{2\cdot\text{Precision}\cdot\text{Recall}}{\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}}, (44)

where T​PTP, T​NTN, F​PFP, and F​NFN denote true positive, true negative, false positive, and false negative classifications, respectively. A​c​c​u​r​a​c​yAccuracy quantifies the proportion of correct predictions across all instances; P​r​e​c​i​s​i​o​nPrecision measures the model’s ability to avoid false positives when identifying present objects; R​e​c​a​l​lRecall assesses the model’s capacity to identify all actually present objects; and F​1−s​c​o​r​eF1-score provides a harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, offering a comprehensive performance metric that balances both dimensions of classification quality.

H.4 MME

MME (Fu et al., 2023a) (Multimodal Model Evaluation) constitutes a comprehensive benchmark for multimodal large language model assessment, encompassing 14 distinct subtasks categorized into perceptual domains (object existence, quantification, color identification, spatial relationships) and cognitive domains (commonsense reasoning, numerical computation, text translation). To facilitate quantitative assessment, MME employs a standardized binary response format analogous to POPE, requiring ”Yes/No” responses. A distinctive characteristic of this framework is its complementary instruction design—each visual input is paired with dual instructions, one requiring an affirmative response and the other a negative response based on ground truth. For evaluation metrics, MME implements an a​c​c​u​r​a​c​yaccuracy-based assessment methodology similar to POPE, calculating performance based on correct classification across individual instructions.

Appendix I Efficiency Comparison

We benchmark inference efficiency on the POPE MSCOCO Random split using LLaVA-1.5 on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 24GB GPU. As shown in Table 8, CD methods roughly double the runtime of regular decoding while incurring only modest additional memory usage. Compared with VCD, VCD+ACD reduces both latency (0.537s→\to0.493s per example) and GPU memory (15.8G→\to15.3G). The savings arise because ACD operates solely on attention maps for hallucination-prone inputs, bypassing the full forward pass through hidden states that VCD requires. This targeted computation enables stronger hallucination suppression at lower overhead, making ACD a more efficient plug-in for practical LVLM deployment.

Appendix J MME Full Set Results

Figure 8 reports scores on the complete MME benchmark using LLaVA-1.5, which exhibits trends representative of the other evaluated models. Compared with vanilla VCD, VCD+ACD yields consistent improvements on both perception and cognition subtasks. The gains are especially pronounced in cognitively demanding categories such as Commonsense Reasoning, OCR, and Text Translation. These results indicate that attention-level contrastive decoding not only preserves core visual understanding but actively strengthens complex reasoning while suppressing hallucinations.

Appendix K Effect of ACD when LVLMs Scale Up

To examine the scalability of our approach, we evaluate ACD on LLaVA-1.5 at both 7B and 13B parameter scales using the LLaVA-Bench-Wild benchmark with GPT-5 as the evaluator (Table 9). VCD+ACD consistently outperforms vanilla VCD across all evaluation categories and model sizes. For the 7B configuration, ACD delivers substantial accuracy gains in Conv (+2.16) and Detail (+3.00) tasks, along with improved descriptive richness. The 13B model exhibits comparable or even larger improvements (+2.40 Conv, +2.98 Detail), with overall accuracy increasing by +1.60 points. Two observations merit emphasis. First, the performance gap between VCD and VCD+ACD persists—and in several categories widens—as model capacity grows. This suggests that attention-level contrastive decoding targets hallucination pathways that architectural scaling alone does not resolve. Second, the Detail scores improve alongside accuracy, indicating that ACD encourages richer, more grounded descriptions rather than conservative short answers. These results confirm that ACD remains effective across model scales and serves as a complementary mechanism to parameter scaling for enhancing vision-language reasoning.

Appendix L Effect of Different Sampling Strategies

The decoding strategy used during text generation governs the trade-off between output determinism and diversity, and may interact with contrastive decoding in non-trivial ways. We therefore ablate ACD under five representative strategies on the CHAIR benchmark with LLaVA-1.5 (Table 10). Greedy search always selects the highest-probability token, yielding deterministic but less diverse outputs. Direct sampling draws from the full vocabulary distribution, increasing diversity at the risk of sampling low-probability noise tokens. Top-kk sampling restricts the candidate set to the kk most probable tokens, suppressing low-probability outliers. Top-pp (nucleus) sampling instead retains the smallest token set whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold pp, allowing the candidate size to adapt to the distribution’s entropy and thus more flexibly balancing coherence with diversity. Finally, top-kk with temperature scaling sharpens the distribution before applying the top-kk constraint, further amplifying high-probability tokens and improving generation stability. As shown in Table 10, ACD consistently reduces both Chairs\text{Chair}_{s} and Chairi\text{Chair}_{i} while improving Recall under every strategy tested. The gains are notably robust: even under greedy decoding, where the baseline is already deterministic, ACD lowers Chairi\text{Chair}_{i} by 1.2 points and raises Recall by 1.8 points. These results confirm that ACD operates as a strategy-agnostic method whose hallucination mitigation benefits are orthogonal to the choice of sampling scheme.

Appendix M Additional Validation Experiments

M.1 ASS Threshold Sensitivity

ASS employs a threshold-free binary mask Mt=𝕀⁡(Atnoisy>Atclean)M_{t}=\mathbb{I}(A_{t}^{\text{noisy}}>A_{t}^{\text{clean}}), using zero as the natural decision boundary. To verify robustness, we generalize the mask to Mt=𝕀⁡(Atnoisy−Atclean>τ)M_{t}=\mathbb{I}(A_{t}^{\text{noisy}}-A_{t}^{\text{clean}}>\tau) and ablate τ\tau on CHAIR (LLaVA-1.5). As shown in Table 11, performance varies by only 0.4 Chairi\text{Chair}_{i} across the full range, confirming that the zero boundary is both near-optimal and highly stable.

M.2 Stratified Analysis: When Does ACD Help Most?

To understand whether ACD primarily prevents collateral damage from logit-level CD or corrects intrinsic hallucinations, we partition CHAIR instances (LLaVA-1.5) by whether the base model already hallucinates. Results are shown in Table 12.

On the “Clean Correct” subset, VCD introduces substantial new hallucinations (Chairi\text{Chair}_{i}: 0→\to8.2) through aggressive logit corruption; ACD nearly halves this collateral damage (8.2→\to4.5, −-45.1%). On the “Clean Hallucinating” subset, ACD provides a smaller but consistent improvement. This confirms that ACD’s primary strength is preventing the coherence degradation that logit-level CD introduces, while offering modest additional correction for intrinsic hallucinations.

M.4 VCD Degeneration on Deeper Architectures

During Qwen3-VL-8B evaluation, we observe that logit-level VCD produces a significant proportion of malformed outputs (Table 15), including infinite non-English token loops and garbled sequences. This failure mode arises because logit subtraction suppresses EOS probability below the penalty threshold in deeper architectures with sharper logit distributions. ACD exhibits zero malformed outputs across all settings, as attention-level intervention preserves the natural token ranking.

Appendix N Case Studies

Case studies on the Chair dataset and LLaVA-bench are presented to illustrate the effectiveness of our approach. Figures9,10, 11, and 12 provides instances of hallucination corrections achieved by our method ACD. From a perceptual standpoint, our method generates more coherent and diverse content while offering supplemental examples of the enhancements brought by our proposed ACD in bolstering the general perception and recognition abilities of LVLMs.
